procedural_history.originating_court: Additional Sessions Judge, Delhi (conducting the trial for the Samastipur Bomb Blast case)
procedural_history.impugned_order: Unclear from the text, but the petitioner seems to be challenging the lack of state-provided legal aid.
procedural_history.high_court_proceedings: The case originated as Writ Petition (Criminal) No. 1792 of 1981 directly in the Supreme Court under Article 32 of the Constitution. There is no mention of prior proceedings in a High Court.
procedural_history.supreme_court_posture: The Supreme Court ultimately dismissed the writ petition, suggesting the petitioner should apply to the Additional Sessions Judge for free legal aid under Section 304 of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973. The Court initially passed interim orders for the State to pay the petitioner's counsel fees, but these were subject to final accounting based on the outcome of the writ petition. The Court later quantified the amount to be paid to the senior and junior counsel.

directions: the writ petition must fail and is dismissed with no order as to costs
the excess amount paid to the petitioner in terms thereof shall not be recoverable

issue.issue_text: Whether a petition under Article 32 of the Constitution is maintainable for a direction to provide counsel for defence at the expense of the State, when the condition is that the trial judge must first be satisfied that the petitioner lacks sufficient means to engage a counsel.

facts: The petitioner, an advocate on trial for murder, filed a petition directly in the Supreme Court under Article 32.
He claimed he did not have sufficient means to hire a competent lawyer to match the 'galaxy of lawyers' hired by the State for the prosecution.
He sought a direction (writ of Mandamus) for the State to provide him with financial assistance to engage a counsel of his choice, with fees comparable to those paid to the prosecution's lawyers.
law: Article 39-A of the Constitution is a Directive Principle of State Policy, which directs the state to provide free legal aid. However, it is not a directly enforceable fundamental right.
The objective of Article 39-A is to be implemented through specific legislation or schemes.
Section 304(1) of the Criminal Procedure Code (Cr.P.C.), 1973, is the specific legislation that provides the procedure for an accused person to obtain free legal aid.
Under Section 304(1) Cr.P.C., the trial court can provide a counsel at the expense of the State if it is satisfied that the accused does not have sufficient means to engage one.
application: The Court determined that a writ of Mandamus under Article 32 cannot be issued to directly enforce a Directive Principle like Article 39-A.

The Court identified that the proper legal remedy for the petitioner was not a constitutional petition, but an application to the trial court (the Additional Sessions Judge) under the specific statutory provision of Section 304(1) Cr.P.C.
It is the role of the trial judge, not the Supreme Court in a writ petition, to first assess the material presented and be satisfied that the petitioner lacks the means to hire a lawyer.
By asking the petitioner to apply to the trial court, the Court upheld the established legal procedure where the trial judge makes the initial determination for granting state-funded legal aid.
reasoning.conclusion: The Supreme Court rejected the petition, holding that it was not maintainable. The Court reasoned that the petitioner's remedy was to apply for free legal aid to the trial judge under Section 304(1) of the Cr.P.C., which is the specific law enacted to fulfill the objective of Article 39-A, rather than seeking direct enforcement of a Directive Principle through an Article 32 petition.

arguments.issue_text: Whether a petition under Article 32 of the Constitution is maintainable for a direction to provide counsel for defence at the expense of the State, when the condition is that the trial judge must first be satisfied that the petitioner lacks sufficient means to engage a counsel.
appellant_arguments: The petitioner, an advocate facing a serious trial, did not have the means to engage a competent lawyer, while the prosecution was represented by a team of lawyers paid large fees by the State.
The fee of Rs. 24 per day fixed by the Delhi High Court for an amicus curiae is grossly insufficient to engage a lawyer of sufficient standing for a long trial.
Article 22(1) and Article 39-A of the Constitution obligate the State to provide the accused with a counsel on a basis of equal opportunity as a matter of processual fair play.
The court should direct the State to provide financial assistance to the petitioner to engage a counsel of his choice.
respondent_arguments: The petition under Article 32 was not maintainable.
The petitioner has no legal right to be supplied with a lawyer by the State, and there is no corresponding obligation on the State to do so.
The petitioner's correct remedy is to make an application under Section 304(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973, before the Court of Sessions.
It is for the trial judge to determine if the petitioner qualifies for free legal aid after being satisfied that the accused lacks sufficient means.

cases.case_name: Janardan Reddy & Ors. v. The State of Hyderabad & Ors.
cases.principle: For the traditional view that the right to be defended by a legal practitioner under Art. 22(1) meant only the right to have an opportunity to engage a lawyer, not an absolute right to be supplied with a lawyer by the State.
For the American 'due process' doctrine regarding the right to counsel, which was previously held not to be applicable to India.

cases.case_name: Maneka Gandhi v. Union of India
cases.principle: For the principle that the requirement of natural justice is implicit in Article 21, and that procedure established by law must be reasonable and not arbitrary, oppressive, or fanciful.

cases.case_name: E. P. Royapa v. State of Tamil Nadu
cases.principle: For the principle that arbitrariness is the antithesis of equality guaranteed under Article 14.

cases.case_name: R. D. Shetty v. The International Airport Authority of India & Ors.
cases.principle: For the principle that an unreasonable procedure cannot be in conformity with Article 14, as the concept of reasonableness permeates that Article.

cases.principle: As one of the later pronouncements that established guidelines for the administration of justice, recognizing the right to legal aid by reading the Directive Principle in Article 39-A with Article 21.

ratio_decidendi.ratio: A writ of Mandamus cannot be granted for the enforcement of the Directive Principle in Article 39A to compel the state to provide financial assistance for an accused to engage a counsel of their choice on a scale equivalent to the fees paid to the state's counsel, as the objective of equal justice and free legal aid under this article is to be implemented through legislation or schemes.
obiter: The traditional interpretation of Article 22(1), which did not guarantee an absolute right to be supplied with a lawyer by the State, has changed with the introduction of Article 39A.
Courts have a responsibility to interpret the Constitution to ensure the implementation of Directive Principles and to harmonize them with Fundamental Rights.
High Courts have the power to fix a reasonable fee for empanelled lawyers in sessions trials and should consider whether existing scales of remuneration are grossly insufficient and require revision.

judicial_reasoning.core_finding: The petitioner is not entitled to the grant of a writ of Mandamus for the enforcement of the Directive Principle enshrined in Art. 39A by ordaining the Union of India to give financial assistance to him to engage a counsel of his choice on a scale equivalent to, or commensurate with, the fees that are being paid to the counsel appearing for the State. The social objective of equal justice and free legal aid has to be implemented by suitable legislation or by formulating schemes for free legal aid, not by a direct court order for financial assistance.
legal_tests_applied: The correct remedy for an accused seeking legal aid at state expense is to make an application before the trial judge, who must be satisfied on material placed before him that the petitioner is not possessed of sufficient means to engage a counsel, as per Section 304(1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure, 1973.
why_appellant_lost: A petition under Article 32 is not maintainable to seek a writ of Mandamus for the enforcement of the Directive Principle in Article 39-A.

The objective of Article 39-A, providing equal justice and free legal aid, is to be implemented by the Legislature and the Executive through legislation or schemes, not by a direct judicial command for financial assistance to an individual.
The petitioner's remedy lies in applying to the trial court, which must first be satisfied that the accused lacks sufficient means to engage counsel before such aid can be ordered.
why_respondent_won: The petitioner has no legal right to be supplied with a lawyer by the State in the manner requested, and there is no corresponding obligation on the State to do so outside the established statutory procedure.
The correct remedy for the petitioner is to make an application before the trial judge under the Code of Criminal Procedure.

It is the duty of the trial judge, not the Supreme Court via a writ petition, to first determine if the petitioner lacks sufficient means to engage a counsel, which is a pre-condition for providing counsel at the expense of the State.
policy_considerations: The traditional view that the right to counsel under Art. 22(1) was merely an opportunity to engage a lawyer has undergone a change with the introduction of Art. 39-A and s. 304(1) of the Cr.P.C.

Read with Article 21, the Directive Principle in Article 39-A has led to the guideline that when an accused is unable to engage a counsel owing to poverty or similar circumstances, the trial would be vitiated unless the State offers free legal aid.

There is no disharmony between Directive Principles and Fundamental Rights; they supplement each other in aiming at the same goal of bringing about a social revolution and the establishment of a welfare State.

Primarily, the mandate in Art. 39A is addressed to the Legislature and the Executive, but courts are also bound by this mandate and have a responsibility to interpret the Constitution to ensure implementation of Directives and harmonize them with individual rights.
